newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-New Bank of France team leaves rates alone.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-New Bank of France team leaves rates alone.

text.p: The Bank of France on Thursday held its key intervention rate unchanged, in what some saw as a sign the independent central bank was sticking to its cautious policy despite the appointment of two new members.

The central bank, whose nine-member monetary policy council held its first meeting since Pierre Guillen and Jean-Rene Bernard joined the policy-setting body this month, said it was leaving its intervention rate at 3.15 percent.
Economists had said the new composition of the council could tip the balance in favour of faster interest rate cuts. But they said on Thursday they still expected monetary easing soon.

"I'd say it's a fairly cautious approach, in part designed to quash speculation the two new council members would instantly advocate looser monetary policy," Sonja Gibbs, bond strategist at Nomura International, said.
"It doesn't change expectations at all for rate cuts in the first quarter, of at least 10 to 15 basis points," she added.
In a Reuter poll on Monday, 10 out of 15 economists said they expected the bank to shave the intervention rate, which sets the floor on money market rates, on Thursday.
"It's slightly disappointing for the market. There were strong expectations built on a rate cut," Philippe Brossard, economist at ABN-Amro, said.
But he said he still believed the bank's council had turned more "dovish" -- softer on monetary policy -- and expected it to try to bring French official rates down to the level of Germany.

The bank has traditionally maintained a small premium over Germany's repo rate, now at 3.00 percent, to cushion the franc against attack on currency markets and to defend its link to the mark, seen as the cornerstone of the European single currency project.
The intervention rate was last cut -- from 3.20 percent -- on December 17, 1996. The bank continued to post its five-to-10 day rate at 4.60 percent.
